claim: Drosophila Piezo is expressed in a rare population of fly neurons that innervate the anterior gut and crop.
source: Here, we identify an essential role for Drosophila Piezo in volume-based control of meal size. We discover a rare population of fly neurons that express Piezo, innervate the anterior gut and crop (a food reservoir organ), and respond to tissue distension in a Piezo-dependent manner.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the discovery of Piezo-expressing neurons innervating the anterior gut and crop, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Piezo-expressing neurons respond to tissue distension in a Piezo-dependent manner.
source: We discover a rare population of fly neurons that express Piezo, innervate the anterior gut and crop (a food reservoir organ), and respond to tissue distension in a Piezo-dependent manner.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by CaLexA reporter experiments shown in Figure 3 demonstrating neuronal responses to gut distension that are abolished in Piezo knockout flies.

claim: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by thermogenetic activation experiments using Trpa1 shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Piezo knockout causes gut bloating.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by crop size measurements in Piezo knockout flies shown in Figure 4.

claim: Piezo knockout increases food consumption.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by feeding assay data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: Piezo knockout increases body weight.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Piezo neuron silencing causes gut bloating.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by Shibire-mediated silencing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Piezo neuron silencing increases food consumption.
source: Activating Piezo neurons decreases appetite, while Piezo knockout and Piezo neuron silencing cause gut bloating and increase both food consumption and body weight.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by feeding index measurements in Shibire experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately 5-6 Piezo-expressing enteric neurons are located in the hypocerebral ganglion per fly.
source: We observed a small group of Piezo-expressing enteric neurons located in the hypocerebral ganglion (~5–6 neurons per fly), and a dense network of Piezo fibers throughout the crop and anterior midgut (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of Piezo neurons observed, supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Piezo fibers form a dense network throughout the crop and anterior midgut.
source: We observed a small group of Piezo-expressing enteric neurons located in the hypocerebral ganglion (~5–6 neurons per fly), and a dense network of Piezo fibers throughout the crop and anterior midgut (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the innervation pattern, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and 1F.

claim: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain approximately 35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry.
source: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain ~35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry, and Piezo neurons therein were distinct from other neurons that expressed the fructose receptor Gr43a (~5 neurons per fly) or the glucagon analog adipokinetic hormone (Akh, ~20 neurons per fly) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the neuron count based on Elav staining, supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Piezo neurons are distinct from Gr43a-expressing neurons in the hypocerebral ganglion.
source: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain ~35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry, and Piezo neurons therein were distinct from other neurons that expressed the fructose receptor Gr43a (~5 neurons per fly) or the glucagon analog adipokinetic hormone (Akh, ~20 neurons per fly) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this distinction, supported by dual labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Piezo neurons are distinct from Akh-expressing neurons in the hypocerebral ganglion.
source: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain ~35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry, and Piezo neurons therein were distinct from other neurons that expressed the fructose receptor Gr43a (~5 neurons per fly) or the glucagon analog adipokinetic hormone (Akh, ~20 neurons per fly) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this distinction, supported by dual labeling experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 5 Gr43a neurons are present per fly in the hypocerebral ganglion region.
source: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain ~35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry, and Piezo neurons therein were distinct from other neurons that expressed the fructose receptor Gr43a (~5 neurons per fly) or the glucagon analog adipokinetic hormone (Akh, ~20 neurons per fly) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this number, supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Approximately 20 Akh neurons are present per fly in the hypocerebral ganglion region.
source: The hypocerebral ganglion and adjacent corpora cardiaca together contain ~35 neurons per fly based on Elav immunohistochemistry, and Piezo neurons therein were distinct from other neurons that expressed the fructose receptor Gr43a (~5 neurons per fly) or the glucagon analog adipokinetic hormone (Akh, ~20 neurons per fly) (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this number, supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Piezo neurites form a muscle-associated lattice in the gut.
source: Piezo neurites formed a muscle-associated lattice in the gut, and ascending axons contributed to the recurrent nerve (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this anatomical feature, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Piezo neuron ascending axons contribute to the recurrent nerve.
source: Piezo neurites formed a muscle-associated lattice in the gut, and ascending axons contributed to the recurrent nerve (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this anatomical feature, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Separate Piezo neurons innervate the crop and/or anterior midgut.
source: Using a genetic approach involving the MultiColor FlpOut system (Nern et al., 2015) for sparse labeling of Piezo cells, flies were obtained with reporter expression in one or a few hypocerebral ganglion neurons but not in brain structures such as the pars intercerebralis; in these flies, separate Piezo neurons were observed to innervate the crop and/or anterior midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding from sparse labeling experiments, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Drosophila Piezo confers mechanically activated currents when expressed in human cells.
source: Drosophila Piezo was previously shown to confer mechanically activated currents when expressed in human cells and to mediate mechanical nociception (Coste et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work (Coste et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012) demonstrating this functional property.

claim: Drosophila Piezo mediates mechanical nociception.
source: Drosophila Piezo was previously shown to confer mechanically activated currents when expressed in human cells and to mediate mechanical nociception (Coste et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work (Coste et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012) demonstrating this functional role.

claim: Vertebrate Piezo homologs play diverse mechanosensory roles, including in internal sensation of airway volume and blood pressure.
source: Furthermore, vertebrate Piezo homologs play diverse mechanosensory roles, including in internal sensation of airway volume and blood pressure (Min et al., 2019; Nonomura et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work (Min et al., 2019; Nonomura et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2018) demonstrating these roles in vertebrates.

claim: Silencing Piezo neurons using Shibire causes flies to feed ravenously.
source: Piezo>Shits flies from all three genotypes fed ravenously, and histological examination of the gastrointestinal tract showed gut bloating with increased crop size (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this behavioral phenotype, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Silencing Piezo neurons using Shibire causes increased crop size.
source: Piezo>Shits flies from all three genotypes fed ravenously, and histological examination of the gastrointestinal tract showed gut bloating with increased crop size (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by crop size measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genetic silencing of GMR51F12-Gal4 neurons does not impact appetite or cause crop distension.
source: For comparison, genetic silencing of other gut-innervating neurons labeled in GMR51F12-Gal4 flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) did not impact appetite or cause crop distension.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this control experiment result, supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Disrupting Piezo neurons compromises gut volume homeostasis and associated control of feeding.
source: These findings indicate that disrupting Piezo neurons compromises gut volume homeostasis and associated control of feeding.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on Shibire silencing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of Piezo neurons using Trpa1 suppresses food intake after a 24-hr fast.
source: Thermogenetic activation of Trpa1 in Piezo cells, achieved by transferring Piezo>Trpa1 flies from 18°C to 30°C, suppressed food intake after a 24-hr fast and also blocked meal-associated increases in crop volume, with similar results observed using three different Piezo-Gal4 drivers (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of Piezo neurons using Trpa1 blocks meal-associated increases in crop volume.
source: Thermogenetic activation of Trpa1 in Piezo cells, achieved by transferring Piezo>Trpa1 flies from 18°C to 30°C, suppressed food intake after a 24-hr fast and also blocked meal-associated increases in crop volume, with similar results observed using three different Piezo-Gal4 drivers (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by crop size measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The relevant Piezo expression site for feeding control is neurons.
source: First, we drove Gal80 expression broadly in neurons using Piezo>Trpa1; Elav-Gal80 flies and observed restoration of normal feeding behavior, indicating the relevant Piezo expression site to be neurons (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on Elav-Gal80 rescue experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cha-Gal80 silences Gal4-mediated expression in the ventral nerve cord and many central neurons, but not in gut-innervating hypocerebral neurons.
source: Differential expression control could be partially achieved using a Cha-Gal80 driver, which silences Gal4-mediated expression in the ventral nerve cord and many central neurons, but not in gut-innervating hypocerebral neurons or a few cells of the proboscis, intestine, and brain (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the expression pattern of Cha-Gal80, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo>Trpa1; Cha-Gal80 flies causes robust suppression of feeding behavior.
source: Thermogenetic experiments in Piezo>Trpa1; Cha-Gal80 flies also caused robust suppression of feeding behavior (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of intestinal cells using Escargot-Gal4; UAS-Trpa1 flies has no effect on feeding.
source: Intestinal cells are unlikely to contribute to feeding phenotypes in Piezo>Trpa1; Cha-Gal80 flies based on experiments involving Piezo>Trpa1; Elav-Gal80 flies; to provide additional evidence, we obtained Escargot-Gal4 flies in which Piezo-expressing intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are broadly marked (He et al., 2018) and found that thermogenetic activation of intestinal cells using Escargot-Gal4; UAS-Trpa1 flies also had no effect on feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this control experiment result, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Piezo neurons expressing Dilp2 in the pars intercerebralis innervate the crop and control feeding behavior.
source: Piezo neurons expressing Dilp2 in the pars intercerebralis are also reported to innervate the crop and control feeding behavior (Wang et al., 2020), which potentially explain the significant differences we observe in feeding following thermogenetic activation experiments involving Piezo-Gal4; UAS-Trpa1 and Piezo-Gal4; UAS-Trpa1; Cha-Gal80 flies (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work (Wang et al., 2020) and uses it to interpret differences in experimental results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, reporter expression is observed in 6.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons per fly.
source: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 6.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 4.9 ± 1.0 pars intercerebralis neurons, 2.9 ± 0.7 of which express Dilp2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, reporter expression is observed in 4.9 ± 1.0 pars intercerebralis neurons per fly.
source: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 6.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 4.9 ± 1.0 pars intercerebralis neurons, 2.9 ± 0.7 of which express Dilp2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, 2.9 ± 0.7 pars intercerebralis neurons express Dilp2.
source: In control Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 6.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 4.9 ± 1.0 pars intercerebralis neurons, 2.9 ± 0.7 of which express Dilp2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, reporter expression is observed in 5.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons per fly.
source: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 5.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 1.1 ± 0.5 pars intercerebralis neuron, 0.4 ± 0.3 of which express Dilp2 (about half of flies had one co-labeled neuron and half had zero) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, reporter expression is observed in 1.1 ± 0.5 pars intercerebralis neurons per fly.
source: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 5.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 1.1 ± 0.5 pars intercerebralis neuron, 0.4 ± 0.3 of which express Dilp2 (about half of flies had one co-labeled neuron and half had zero) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, 0.4 ± 0.3 pars intercerebralis neurons express Dilp2.
source: In Piezo-Gal4; UAS-CD8RFP; Cha-Gal80 flies, we observed reporter expression per fly in 5.2 ± 0.5 hypocerebral neurons and 1.1 ± 0.5 pars intercerebralis neuron, 0.4 ± 0.3 of which express Dilp2 (about half of flies had one co-labeled neuron and half had zero) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this quantification, supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Dilp2-Gal4 does not label Elav-marked hypocerebral neurons.
source: Furthermore, Dilp2-Gal4 does not label Elav-marked hypocerebral neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Both hypocerebral and pars intercerebralis Piezo neurons contribute to feeding control.
source: Additional studies are needed to distinguish the contributions of hypocerebral and pars intercerebralis Piezo neurons, with data so far suggesting that both subtypes of Piezo neurons contribute to feeding control.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the experimental data from Figures 2 and 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Trpa1-induced activation of Piezo neurons increases CaLexA reporter levels gradually, with maximal induction by 24 hr.
source: For validation and determination of response kinetics, Trpa1-induced activation of Piezo neurons increased CaLexA reporter levels gradually, with maximal induction by 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by time-course data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CaLexA-driven GFP expression in hypocerebral Piezo neurons is low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum.
source: For both neuron types, we observed that CaLexA-driven GFP expression was low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum, but was strikingly elevated when flies engorged themselves on a sucrose diet (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CaLexA-driven GFP expression in hypocerebral Piezo neurons is strikingly elevated when flies engorge themselves on a sucrose diet.
source: For both neuron types, we observed that CaLexA-driven GFP expression was low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum, but was strikingly elevated when flies engorged themselves on a sucrose diet (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CaLexA-driven GFP expression in hypocerebral Gr43a neurons is low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum.
source: For both neuron types, we observed that CaLexA-driven GFP expression was low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum, but was strikingly elevated when flies engorged themselves on a sucrose diet (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CaLexA-driven GFP expression in hypocerebral Gr43a neurons is strikingly elevated when flies engorge themselves on a sucrose diet.
source: For both neuron types, we observed that CaLexA-driven GFP expression was low after a fast or in flies fed ad libitum, but was strikingly elevated when flies engorged themselves on a sucrose diet (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sucrose consumption increases crop volume compared with flies fed ad libitum.
source: Sucrose consumption could potentially stimulate both gut chemosensors and mechanosensors as an increase in crop volume was observed compared with flies fed ad libitum (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by crop size measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Enteric Gr43a neurons display elevated levels of CaLexA-mediated GFP expression after engorgement on sucrose, but not sucralose or water.
source: Enteric Gr43a neurons displayed elevated levels of CaLexA-mediated GFP expression after engorgement on sucrose, which is converted into fructose and glucose, but not sucralose or water, consistent with a role for these neurons in sensing nutritional carbohydrates (Miyamoto and Amrein, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Enteric Piezo neurons are activated by sucrose, sucralose, and deprivation-induced water ingestion, but not in controls given only water ad libitum.
source: In contrast, enteric Piezo neurons were activated more generally by sucrose, sucralose, and deprivation-induced water ingestion, but not in controls given only water ad libitum, with responses correlated to the extent of gut distension.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Piezo neuron responses are correlated to the extent of gut distension.
source: In contrast, enteric Piezo neurons were activated more generally by sucrose, sucralose, and deprivation-induced water ingestion, but not in controls given only water ad libitum, with responses correlated to the extent of gut distension.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this correlation, supported by CaLexA reporter data and crop size measurements shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Piezo neurons are similarly activated by water- and sucrose-induced gut distension.
source: The observation that Piezo neurons were similarly activated by water- and sucrose-induced gut distension indicated a sensory mechanism that does not require chemosensation of particular nutrients.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Piezo neuron activation does not require chemosensation of particular nutrients.
source: The observation that Piezo neurons were similarly activated by water- and sucrose-induced gut distension indicated a sensory mechanism that does not require chemosensation of particular nutrients.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There are two segregated sensory pathways through the hypocerebral ganglion, with Gr43a neurons responding to sugars and Piezo neurons responding to anterior gut mechanosensation.
source: Together, these findings suggest a model of two segregated sensory pathways through the hypocerebral ganglion, with Gr43a neurons responding to sugars and Piezo neurons responding to anterior gut mechanosensation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this model based on CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Hypocerebral ganglion neurons marked in Piezo-Gal4 flies but lacking Piezo expression do not respond to engorgement by sucrose, sucralose, or water.
source: Remarkably, hypocerebral ganglion neurons marked in Piezo-Gal4 flies but lacking Piezo expression did not respond to engorgement by sucrose, sucralose, or water, even though the crops of Piezo knockout flies were distended (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The crops of Piezo knockout flies are distended after engorgement.
source: Remarkably, hypocerebral ganglion neurons marked in Piezo-Gal4 flies but lacking Piezo expression did not respond to engorgement by sucrose, sucralose, or water, even though the crops of Piezo knockout flies were distended (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation, supported by crop size measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies is sufficient to induce a CaLexA-mediated response.
source: A lack of neuronal responses in Piezo knockout flies is not due to gross deficits in the ability to produce reporter as Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies was sufficient to induce a CaLexA-mediated response (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this control experiment result, supported by CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Piezo neurons still innervate the anterior gut in Piezo knockout flies.
source: Furthermore, Piezo neurons still innervated the anterior gut, suggesting that the deficit was not due to coarse developmental miswiring (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Enteric neurons of Piezo knockout flies fail to respond to crop-distending stimuli due to a mechanosensory defect.
source: Instead, enteric neurons of Piezo knockout flies seemingly fail to respond to crop-distending stimuli due to a mechanosensory defect.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on CaLexA reporter data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Piezo knockout flies increase food intake compared to isogenic w1118 flies.
source: Remarkably, Piezo knockout flies increased food intake and had visually observable crop distension (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Piezo knockout flies have visually observable crop distension.
source: Remarkably, Piezo knockout flies increased food intake and had visually observable crop distension (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by imaging and crop size measurements shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Piezo knockout flies fed ad libitum on normal fly food for 5–7 days show an increase in body weight compared to control flies.
source: Moreover, Piezo knockout flies fed ad libitum on normal fly food for 5–7 days showed an increase in body weight compared to control flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Piezo knockout flies display an increase in food intake compared to wild-type flies.
source: Automated analysis of feeding patterns was performed involving an EXPRESSO platform (Yapici et al., 2016), and Piezo knockout flies displayed an increase in food intake and feeding bout duration but a similar frequency of feeding bout initiation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by EXPRESSO assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Piezo knockout flies display an increase in feeding bout duration compared to wild-type flies.
source: Automated analysis of feeding patterns was performed involving an EXPRESSO platform (Yapici et al., 2016), and Piezo knockout flies displayed an increase in food intake and feeding bout duration but a similar frequency of feeding bout initiation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by EXPRESSO assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Piezo knockout flies display a similar frequency of feeding bout initiation compared to wild-type flies.
source: Automated analysis of feeding patterns was performed involving an EXPRESSO platform (Yapici et al., 2016), and Piezo knockout flies displayed an increase in food intake and feeding bout duration but a similar frequency of feeding bout initiation (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by EXPRESSO assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Abnormal gut distension and feeding behavior in Piezo knockout flies are rescued by exogenous expression of Piezo-GFP in Piezo knockout neurons driven by Piezo-Gal4.
source: Abnormal gut distension and feeding behavior were rescued by exogenous expression of Piezo-GFP in Piezo knockout neurons driven by Piezo-Gal4 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this rescue experiment result, supported by feeding index and crop size data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Piezo knockout flies have normal food transit.
source: Unlike Drop-dead knockout flies that have an enlarged crop due to defective food passage into the intestine (Peller et al., 2009), Piezo knockout flies have normal food transit, a normal lifespan, and increased defecation rates, presumably due to increased feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by intestinal transit data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Piezo knockout flies have a normal lifespan.
source: Unlike Drop-dead knockout flies that have an enlarged crop due to defective food passage into the intestine (Peller et al., 2009), Piezo knockout flies have normal food transit, a normal lifespan, and increased defecation rates, presumably due to increased feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Piezo knockout flies have increased defecation rates, presumably due to increased feeding.
source: Unlike Drop-dead knockout flies that have an enlarged crop due to defective food passage into the intestine (Peller et al., 2009), Piezo knockout flies have normal food transit, a normal lifespan, and increased defecation rates, presumably due to increased feeding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by fecal spot deposition data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The anatomy of the crop appears normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by histology of crop muscle.
source: Other than food-induced distension, the anatomy of the crop appeared normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by histology of crop muscle, analysis of cell density, and volume measurements during starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by muscle fiber density data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The anatomy of the crop appears normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by analysis of cell density.
source: Other than food-induced distension, the anatomy of the crop appeared normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by histology of crop muscle, analysis of cell density, and volume measurements during starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by cell density data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The anatomy of the crop appears normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by volume measurements during starvation.
source: Other than food-induced distension, the anatomy of the crop appeared normal in Piezo knockout flies as visualized by histology of crop muscle, analysis of cell density, and volume measurements during starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by crop size measurements during fasting shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Knockout of Piezo does not impact the extent of gut innervation.
source: As mentioned above, knockout of Piezo does not impact the extent of gut innervation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E); furthermore, thermogenetic Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies suppressed feeding behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), indicating that neural circuits downstream of enteric Piezo neurons were intact and remained capable of eliciting a behavioral response after Piezo knockout.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Thermogenetic Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies suppresses feeding behavior.
source: As mentioned above, knockout of Piezo does not impact the extent of gut innervation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E); furthermore, thermogenetic Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies suppressed feeding behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), indicating that neural circuits downstream of enteric Piezo neurons were intact and remained capable of eliciting a behavioral response after Piezo knockout.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding, supported by feeding index data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Neural circuits downstream of enteric Piezo neurons are intact and remain capable of eliciting a behavioral response after Piezo knockout.
source: As mentioned above, knockout of Piezo does not impact the extent of gut innervation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E); furthermore, thermogenetic Trpa1-mediated activation of Piezo neurons in Piezo knockout flies suppressed feeding behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), indicating that neural circuits downstream of enteric Piezo neurons were intact and remained capable of eliciting a behavioral response after Piezo knockout.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on Trpa1 activation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Piezo functions to guide the differentiation of gut enteroendocrine cells from mechanosensitive ISCs.
source: Piezo also functions to guide the differentiation of gut enteroendocrine cells from mechanosensitive ISCs (He et al., 2018); however, selectively restoring Piezo expression in ISCs using Escargot-Gal4 (Esg-Gal4) did not rescue crop volume and feeding phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
